13090:
To purvey means to supply or provide something — but not in a casual, one-off way. It carries the sense of doing so regularly, professionally, or as an established role. Think of it as a more formal, deliberate kind of providing.

The simplest test: if someone purveys something, they are in the business of making it available to others, consistently and intentionally.

Sense 1 — To supply goods (especially food, drink, or provisions)

This is the oldest and most traditional meaning. It describes the act of sourcing and supplying goods — historically food and drink — to people, establishments, or institutions.

"The family has been purveying fine cheeses to restaurants in the city for over a century."

"The company purveys organic vegetables to schools and hospitals across the region."

Notice that in both examples, the supply is not random or accidental. There is an ongoing, professional relationship between the supplier and the recipient. The word implies a certain established presence in that role.

This is why you often see the related noun purveyor used in formal or high-end commercial contexts — "Purveyor of Fine Foods" — because it signals that someone is not just selling things occasionally, but is dedicated to that supply as their function.

Sense 2 — To spread or circulate ideas, information, content, or culture

In its extended modern use, purvey moves beyond physical goods. It can describe the act of putting out or spreading ideas, stories, information, entertainment, propaganda, or anything that is distributed to an audience.

"That channel has been purveying misinformation for years."

"She built her career purveying escapist romantic fiction to millions of readers."

"The regime used state television to purvey its ideology to the population."

Here, the word still carries the same core flavour — it is systematic, deliberate, and ongoing. You don't purvey something by accident. There is always an intentional, sustained effort behind it.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Purvey is a formal word. You would not hear it in casual conversation. Nobody says "I purveyed some snacks to my friends." In everyday speech, people say provide, supply, sell, or distribute.

You encounter purvey in:

  • Formal business or commercial writing ("purveying luxury goods to discerning clients")
  • Journalism or criticism ("a media outlet that purveys outrage for profit")
  • Literary or elevated prose ("he spent his life purveying half-truths")

When a writer chooses purvey over provide or supply, they are adding a subtle layer of meaning — suggesting that the act is deliberate, professional, and part of an established pattern, rather than something casual or accidental.
What Makes It Different from Simple Synonyms

You might wonder: why not just say supply or provide? Here is the key distinction:

  • Supply / provide are neutral and general. They say nothing about the nature of the relationship or the role of the person doing it.
  • Purvey implies that the person doing it is in a recognised or established capacity as a supplier or distributor. It suggests they are the dedicated source of something for others.

Similarly, compared to sell:

  • Sell focuses on the commercial transaction (money changes hands).
  • Purvey focuses on the role of being the one who makes something available — whether for profit or not.

When purvey is used in Sense 2 — spreading ideas or content — it very often carries a slightly critical or disapproving tone, particularly when the thing being purveyed is undesirable.

"They have long been purveying conspiracy theories to a vulnerable audience."
"The tabloid purveys gossip and scandal."

This is not a strict rule — purvey can be neutral or even positive — but be aware that when a writer uses it to describe the spreading of information or ideas, there is often a quiet suggestion that the thing being purveyed is not entirely respectable, or that the act of spreading it is somewhat cynical.

What it meansTo supply or provide something on a regular, deliberate, professional basis
Physical senseSupplying goods (especially food/drink) to customers or institutions
Abstract senseSpreading ideas, information, content, or culture to an audience
Key flavourFormal; implies an established, ongoing role as a supplier
Tone when abstractOften slightly critical or disapproving
One Sentence to Remember It By

To purvey is to be the consistent, deliberate source from which something flows to others — whether that something is bread, beliefs, or propaganda.

Master that idea and you will read purvey correctly in any context you ever encounter it.
13091:
A purveyor is someone — a person, a business, or an organization — that regularly supplies or provides something, typically as their main activity or profession.

The "something" can be almost anything: physical goods, services, information, or even ideas and culture.

Think of it this way: if someone makes it their business to consistently give, sell, or spread something to others, they are a purveyor of that thing.

The word carries a slightly formal, elevated tone. It's not wrong to say "seller" or "supplier" in most cases — but "purveyor" suggests a sense of specialization, regularity, and sometimes even prestige in what is being provided.
The classic use: goods and provisions

The most traditional use of "purveyor" is for a person or business that supplies goods — especially food, drinks, or other material items — often to a specific customer, institution, or the public.

Examples:

  • A cheese shop that supplies high-quality cheeses to restaurants → a purveyor of fine cheeses
  • A company that provides fresh produce to a five-star hotel → a purveyor of organic ingredients
  • A wine merchant who stocks rare bottles → a purveyor of premium wines

Notice how "purveyor" here implies they aren't just casually selling something once. They do it consistently, often with some level of expertise or quality attached to their name.

A side note worth knowing: In British tradition, businesses that regularly supply goods to the royal family are sometimes officially called "Purveyors by Appointment to His/Her Majesty." This is considered a mark of prestige. This cultural connection has given the word a slightly grand, quality-associated flavor — one that survives in how the word is used even today.
The broader, modern use: information, ideas, and culture

Today, "purveyor" is used far beyond just physical goods. You'll frequently see it applied to intangible things — information, beliefs, values, entertainment, or even attitudes.

Examples:

  • A popular news channel → a purveyor of daily news
  • A comedian who always pokes fun at political figures → a purveyor of political satire
  • A storyteller who passes down cultural legends → a purveyor of folklore
  • Someone who spreads unverified rumors online → a purveyor of misinformation

The word works in all of these cases because the underlying idea is the same: they are regularly and deliberately putting something out into the world.
The tone and connotation: neutral, but flexible

"Purveyor" is a neutral word on its own — it doesn't automatically praise or criticize. Its tone shifts entirely depending on what is being purveyed.

  • "Purveyor of artisan chocolates" → sounds prestigious, admirable
  • "Purveyor of fine literature" → sounds cultured and respected
  • "Purveyor of cheap gossip" → sounds dismissive, slightly critical
  • "Purveyor of hate and division" → sounds strongly negative

The word itself is just pointing at a role. The judgment comes from the object that follows it.
How it differs from similar words

You might wonder: why not just say "seller," "supplier," or "provider"?

  • Seller / vendor — purely transactional. Focused on the act of exchanging money for something. No implication of expertise or specialization.
  • Supplier — often used in a business-to-business, logistical sense. More mechanical and less elegant.
  • Purveyor — carries a sense of expertise, regularity, and a certain identity built around what is provided. It suggests this is not a one-off thing; it's what they do. The word also fits naturally when the thing being provided is intangible (ideas, culture, information), whereas "supplier" feels awkward in those cases.
Putting it all together: a working mental image

Imagine a person who stands at the center of a town square, and every single day, they bring something to the people around them — whether it's bread, wine, stories, knowledge, or opinions. They've made it their thing. People know them for it. They do it consistently and with a certain sense of ownership and identity over what they provide.

That person is a purveyor.

• The café positioned itself as a purveyor of locally sourced, specialty coffee.
  • The professor was seen as a purveyor of radical but intellectually rigorous ideas.
  • The company has long been a purveyor of budget-friendly electronics.
  • The tabloid was criticized for being a purveyor of sensationalist and unverified stories.
  • He set up a small shop as a purveyor of handmade leather goods.

A purveyor is someone who regularly and professionally supplies something — whether goods, services, information, or ideas — and has essentially made that activity their identity or role. The word is formal and slightly elevated in tone, and it can describe both tangible things (food, products) and intangible ones (beliefs, culture, news). The word itself is neutral; whether it sounds positive or negative depends entirely on what is being purveyed.
13092:
Purview means the range, scope, or extent of what something — or someone — is responsible for, has authority over, or is legitimately concerned with.

Imagine an invisible circle drawn around a person, a department, an institution, or a law. Everything inside that circle is their purview — their territory to handle, decide on, or care about. Everything outside that circle is not their purview — it's not their place to touch.

It is a formal word. You won't hear it in casual conversation, but you'll encounter it frequently in professional, legal, academic, and governmental contexts.

1. Scope of authority or responsibility

This is the most common use. When something is "within someone's purview," it means it falls under their authority or is their responsibility to deal with. When something is "outside their purview," it means it simply isn't their job or their call to make.

  • A hospital's medical ethics board has the power to approve or reject experimental treatments. Deciding the hospital's marketing budget is not within their purview — that belongs to management.
  • The fire department's purview is fire safety and emergency rescue. Investigating a theft is the police's purview, not theirs.
  • A school principal's purview includes discipline, curriculum, and staff — but rewriting the national education policy is well beyond their purview.

Notice the pattern: purview defines the boundary of legitimate involvement. It tells you where your authority starts and where it ends.

2. Range of awareness or understanding

Purview can also describe the limits of what someone is aware of, exposed to, or capable of perceiving — not because of a rule, but because of their position, knowledge, or experience.

  • For most people living in the 1800s, events happening on the other side of the world never entered their purview — they simply had no way of knowing.
  • The intricacies of quantum physics fall outside the purview of most non-scientists — not because they're forbidden from it, but because it lies beyond their exposure and understanding.

Here, purview isn't about authority — it's about the limits of someone's world or awareness.

3. The legal sense

In law, the purview of a statute (a written law) refers to what that law actually covers and intends to regulate. If something falls within the purview of a law, the law applies to it. If it falls outside, the law doesn't govern it.

  • A consumer protection law might have a purview that covers only individual buyers, not large corporations buying from other corporations.
  • A court may rule that a certain type of dispute falls outside the purview of a particular regulation, meaning that regulation simply doesn't apply to it.
The Phrases You'll Always See It In

Purview almost always appears with one of these constructions:

"Within the purview of" — it belongs to, it is covered by, it is their responsibility.

Reviewing employee performance is within the purview of the HR department.

"Outside/beyond the purview of" — it doesn't belong to them, it's not their territory.

Personal lifestyle choices are generally outside the purview of an employer.

"Under the purview of" — subject to the authority or supervision of.

Food safety standards fall under the purview of the national health authority.

"The purview of [something]" — the defined scope belonging to that thing.

The committee expanded its purview to include cybersecurity issues.
How Purview Differs From Similar Words

These three words are close neighbors, and understanding the difference will sharpen your use of purview:

Purview vs. Scope
Scope is a more neutral word that simply means the range or extent of something — a project's scope, the scope of a study. Purview carries the extra sense of legitimate claim or authority. It's not just what something covers, but what something has the right to cover or act on.

Purview vs. Jurisdiction
Jurisdiction specifically refers to the official legal authority of courts, governments, or law enforcement. Purview is broader and less formal in the sense that it can apply to any person, role, subject, or organization — not just official legal bodies.

Purview vs. Domain
Domain refers to a general area of knowledge or activity (the domain of science, the domain of art). Purview emphasizes the limits and boundaries of that area more explicitly, and it more strongly implies authority or responsibility within those limits.

Purview is the defined territory — whether of authority, responsibility, or awareness — that belongs to a person, institution, law, or subject: what falls inside it is their business to handle or know; what falls outside it is not.
13093:
Someone who is pushy tries very hard to get what they want — and in doing so, they pressure, rush, or impose on other people without caring much about how those people feel.

A pushy person does not simply ask once and wait politely. They keep pushing — again and again — until the other person gives in, feels uncomfortable, or simply says yes just to make it stop.
Breaking It Down With a Simple Picture

Imagine you are browsing in a clothes shop. A salesperson walks up and says, "Can I help you?" You say, "No thanks, I'm just looking." A normal salesperson smiles and steps back.

A pushy salesperson does not step back. They follow you around the shop. They hold up items and say, "This would look great on you!" You say you're not interested. They lower the price. You still say no. They offer a free gift. They keep going. They make you feel cornered.

That salesperson is pushy.
What Makes Someone Pushy — The Key Ingredients

There are three things that almost always come together when we call someone pushy:

1. They want something from you — a decision, a purchase, an agreement, your time, your attention.

2. They do not respect your "no" or your hesitation — they treat your resistance as a temporary obstacle, not as a valid response.

3. They apply pressure — through persistence, guilt, urgency ("You need to decide NOW!"), flattery, or simply by not leaving you alone.

None of these alone is necessarily pushy. But together, they create the feeling that someone is trying to bulldoze you into agreeing with them.
The Tone: Is "Pushy" a Compliment or an Insult?

"Pushy" is almost always negative. When you call someone pushy, you are criticising them. You are saying they crossed a line — they went from being assertive and confident into being aggressive and disrespectful of your space or wishes.

However, it's worth noting a subtle point: sometimes people say "you need to be a little pushy in this industry" as mild advice — meaning you need to be bold and not too passive. But even here, they are acknowledging that the word sits at the uncomfortable edge of acceptable behaviour. It is never a straightforward compliment.
How Pushy Differs from Similar Words

English has several words for people who try hard to get what they want. It helps to see how pushy sits among them:

Assertive — This is positive. An assertive person states their needs clearly and confidently, but they also accept when the answer is no. They respect others.

Persistent — This is neutral. A persistent person keeps trying over time, but without necessarily pressuring or annoying others. A scientist who runs 500 experiments before finding an answer is persistent, not pushy.

Pushy — This is negative. A pushy person goes past persistence into pressure. They do not respect the other person's boundaries or feelings. They create discomfort.

Aggressive — This is strongly negative and more intense than pushy. Aggressive behaviour can involve anger, threats, or confrontation. Pushiness is more subtle — it is social pressure, not outright hostility.

So the scale roughly goes: assertive → persistent → pushy → aggressive. Pushy sits in the zone where healthy confidence has turned into unwanted pressure.

In sales and business:
A pushy salesman calls you every day after you said you'd think about it. A pushy recruiter keeps emailing even after you said you're not interested.

In social situations:
A pushy friend keeps insisting you come to a party even after you've declined three times. A pushy relative keeps asking when you're getting married even after you've clearly said you don't want to talk about it.

In relationships:
A pushy partner pressures you into making a decision — about where to live, about plans, about commitment — before you are ready, and does not comfortably accept "I need more time."

In negotiations:
Someone who keeps raising objections, changing the terms, and not letting a conversation naturally close can be described as pushy.

• "I asked for time to think about it, but the agent was so pushy that I felt pressured into signing the contract on the spot."
  • "She's very talented, but her pushy attitude at networking events makes people want to avoid her."
  • "Don't be pushy — just tell him once, and if he says no, let it go."
  • "The pushy salesman followed me from aisle to aisle and wouldn't take no for an answer."
  • "I know you want the job, but calling them every day will make you look pushy, not enthusiastic."
The Feeling Pushy Creates in Others

This is important: pushiness is defined not just by the person doing it, but by the feeling it creates in the person receiving it. When someone is being pushy towards you, you typically feel:

  • Cornered — like you have no easy way out
  • Pressured — like you must decide now, even if you're not ready
  • Annoyed or irritated — because they are not listening to you
  • Guilty (sometimes) — like saying no makes you the bad person
  • Disrespected — because your boundaries are being ignored

This emotional effect is part of what makes pushiness different from simple persistence. Persistence may be tiresome; pushiness makes the other person feel that their "no" is not being treated as real.
An Important Nuance: Intent vs. Perception

Here's something subtle but useful to know: a person can be pushy without realising it. They may genuinely believe they are just being enthusiastic, helpful, or thorough. But if the person on the receiving end feels pressured and disrespected, the behaviour is still pushy — regardless of the intent.

This is why "pushy" often describes a person's manner and effect on others, not just their private intentions.

Pushy describes a person who applies unwanted pressure on others to get what they want — ignoring hesitation, brushing off "no," and prioritising their own goals over the other person's comfort and boundaries.
13094:
Pusillanimity is the quality of being weak-spirited, cowardly, and timid — especially when a situation calls for courage, decisiveness, or standing up for what is right. A person who displays pusillanimity tends to shrink, cave, or back down not because the situation is truly overwhelming, but because they lack the inner strength and moral backbone to face it.

Think of it as a smallness of spirit. The word doesn't just mean being afraid. It means being so dominated by fear, self-preservation, or a desire to avoid discomfort that you fail to do what you know is right or necessary.
What Makes It Different From Ordinary Cowardice?

"Cowardice" and "pusillanimity" are close cousins, but pusillanimity is more specific and, in many ways, more damning.

Cowardice is primarily about fear — a soldier running from battle, for instance. It's reactive. Something scary happens, and the person flees.

Pusillanimity, on the other hand, is about a fundamental weakness of character. It's less about a single panicked reaction and more about a persistent, ingrained pattern of avoiding anything difficult, uncomfortable, or risky — even when the stakes are moral rather than physical. It implies a kind of pettiness and smallness alongside the fear.

A coward might be forgiven for panicking in a terrifying moment. A pusillanimous person has no such excuse — they are simply too weak-willed and self-concerned to act with integrity.

When someone accuses another person of pusillanimity, the accusation carries a particular flavor. It suggests that the person:

  • Knows the right thing to do, but refuses to do it out of fear or self-interest.
  • Caves under pressure easily, even when they shouldn't.
  • Avoids taking clear stands, preferring vague, non-committal positions to protect themselves.
  • Prioritizes their own comfort or safety over duty, principle, or the wellbeing of others.

It is a word that belongs to the world of moral judgment. You wouldn't use it to describe a child afraid of the dark. You would use it to describe an adult who, fully knowing what is right, chooses the path of least resistance instead.

Example 1 — The Silent Witness
A manager watches a senior colleague bully and humiliate a junior employee repeatedly. The manager knows it's wrong. They have the authority to stop it. But they say nothing, because confronting the senior colleague might create tension, put their own career at risk, or simply make their working life uncomfortable. That silence, that refusal to act despite knowing better — that is pusillanimity.

Example 2 — The Spineless Leader
A politician privately believes a certain policy is harmful and unjust. When the time comes to vote, they vote in favor of it anyway, because voting against it might cost them popularity, party support, or re-election. They have sacrificed their principles at the altar of self-preservation. This is a textbook case of pusillanimity.

Example 3 — The Hollow Friend
Your friend is being treated unfairly and asks you to speak up on their behalf to someone in power. You know they are right. You agree with them completely. But you stay quiet because you don't want to rock the boat or invite any criticism toward yourself. You later offer your friend private sympathy but public silence. That is pusillanimity.

In all three cases, notice the common thread: the person knows what courage demands of them, and they deliberately choose the weaker path.

To sharpen the definition further, it helps to know what this word does not mean.

  • It is not the same as introversion or shyness. Being quiet or reserved by nature is not pusillanimity. Pusillanimity is specifically about moral and personal courage, not personality type.
  • It is not the same as reasonable caution. Choosing not to pick a fight you cannot possibly win is wisdom, not pusillanimity. The word implies a failure that could and should have been avoided.
  • It is not always about physical fear. In fact, pusillanimity most often shows up in moral, social, or professional situations — places where physical danger is not involved at all, but where integrity is tested.
  • It is not the same as humility. A humble person defers to others because they genuinely respect them. A pusillanimous person defers because they lack the courage to do otherwise.

Pusillanimity is not a casual insult. It is a serious moral charge. When great thinkers, writers, or leaders have used this word across history, they have used it to describe one of the most disappointing things a person can be — not evil, not stupid, but small. Unwilling to rise to the occasion when it matters.

There is something almost sadder about pusillanimity than about outright villainy. The villain at least acts. The pusillanimous person simply... doesn't. They see, they understand, and they shrink.

If you had to capture the entire meaning of pusillanimity in one sentence, it would be this:

Pusillanimity is the quality of being so weak in spirit and so driven by self-preservation that you consistently fail to act with the courage, decisiveness, and integrity that the moment demands of you.
13095:
Pusillanimous means showing a shameful lack of courage or willpower — being so weak in character that you avoid anything difficult, risky, or confrontational, even when the situation genuinely calls for bravery or decisiveness.

In plain terms: a pusillanimous person is a coward — but not just in the physical sense. They are a coward in spirit.
What Makes It Different From Simply Being "Scared"

This is the most important thing to understand. Everyone feels fear. Fear is normal and human. A person can be terrified and still act bravely. That is not pusillanimous.

Pusillanimous describes someone who surrenders to their fear or weakness in a way that is morally contemptible — especially when others are depending on them, or when something important is at stake. It's about a failure of character, not just a feeling.

Think of it this way: a soldier who is scared but still charges forward is brave. A soldier who is scared, sees that people need help, and slinks away anyway — that is pusillanimous.
The Moral Sting in the Word

This word carries a strong negative judgment. When you call someone or something pusillanimous, you are not just describing them — you are disapproving of them, even looking down on them. It implies a smallness and pettiness of spirit.

It can describe:

  • A person who consistently avoids taking a stand or facing hard things
  • A decision or action that is half-hearted, weak, or disgracefully timid
  • A response that dodges difficulty when boldness was needed

Pusillanimous is a fairly formal, literary word. You'll see it more in writing than in everyday conversation. It's especially common in:

  • Political commentary — criticizing leaders who fail to act decisively or take a moral stand
  • Literary or historical writing — describing characters or figures who lack backbone
  • Formal criticism — calling out an organization, institution, or policy for being spineless

These examples will show you exactly how the word works in context:

  1. "The senator's pusillanimous refusal to vote on the bill — out of fear of upsetting donors — outraged his constituents." (He had a moral duty to act, but cowardice won.)
  2. "She gave a pusillanimous apology that admitted nothing and satisfied no one." (The apology was so weak and evasive it was almost an insult in itself.)
  3. "History will not be kind to those who offered a pusillanimous response when decisive action was needed." (A moment called for courage; they delivered weakness.)
  4. "Stop being so pusillanimous and just tell your boss what you actually think." (Said in frustration to someone who keeps backing down from honest confrontation.)
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing where it sits among its neighbors:

  • Timid — mild. A timid person is shy and hesitant by nature. No strong blame is attached. A child can be timid; that's okay.
  • Cowardly — strong. Very close to pusillanimous, but cowardly can describe a single act ("a cowardly attack from behind"). Pusillanimous tends to describe a pattern or quality of character — it feels more like a deep-seated failing than a single bad moment.
  • Faint-hearted — moderate. Similar idea, but softer and less condemnatory than pusillanimous.
  • Spineless — strong and vivid. Very close in meaning. Spineless is more casual and punchy; pusillanimous is more formal and carries an air of measured contempt.
  • Gutless — very casual, blunt, and angry. Pusillanimous is the word you use when you want to sound more considered and authoritative in your condemnation.

Pusillanimous is the most formal and arguably the most cutting of these, because it sounds deliberate and considered — like a verdict, not just an insult flung in the heat of the moment.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

Pusillanimous = weak and cowardly in a way that is morally shameful — not just scared, but too spineless to do what is right or necessary when it truly matters.

If you ever use this word or read it, that judgment — that quiet but sharp contempt for weakness of character — is always present in it.
13096: Before diving in, let's quickly clarify what a phrasal verb is. A phrasal verb is a verb combined with one or more small words (like off, up, out, in) that together create a new meaning — a meaning that is often completely different from the original verb. For example, "put" means to place something somewhere, but "put off" means something entirely different. This is what makes phrasal verbs tricky, and why you need to learn them as whole units.
"Put Off" — The Core Idea

There is one simple image that connects almost all meanings of "put off": the idea of something being pushed away — either in time, or in feeling. Keep this image in mind, and the meanings will make much more sense.
Meaning 1: To Postpone (Delay Something to a Later Time)

This is the most common meaning.

When you put something off, you decide not to do it now and move it to a later time. You are essentially "pushing it away" into the future.

Examples:

  • "I have a dentist appointment tomorrow, but I'm going to put it off until next month." (I'll reschedule it for later.)
  • "She keeps putting off her homework and then panics at night."
  • "Don't put off important decisions — they don't disappear on their own."
  • "The match was put off because of heavy rain." (It was postponed.)

In everyday life, this meaning shows up constantly. Whenever people delay doing something unpleasant or difficult, they are "putting it off." Paying bills, having a hard conversation, going to the doctor — these are all things people commonly put off.

A famous saying you should know:

"Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today."

This is one of the most well-known English proverbs, and now you understand it perfectly.
Meaning 2: To Make Someone Lose Interest, Enthusiasm, or Appetite

This is the second most important meaning, and it is very different from the first. Here, "put off" means to repel, discourage, or disgust someone — to make them not want something anymore.

Think of it like pushing someone away from something emotionally.

Examples:

  • "The terrible smell put me off my food." (I lost my appetite because of it.)
  • "His rude behavior put her off immediately." (She lost interest in him.)
  • "The long waiting lines put me off visiting the museum."
  • "I was going to apply for the job, but the low salary put me off."

Notice that this meaning can work in two slightly different ways:

a) Someone is put off by something (a person, a thing, or a situation causes the feeling):

  • "I was put off by his arrogance."

b) Something puts you off doing something (you stop wanting to do a specific thing):

  • "The accident put me off driving for months."
  • "That bad experience put me off eating seafood."

Both are natural and very common.
Meaning 3: To Cause Someone to Dislike Something (Often Permanently)

This is closely related to Meaning 2, but the result is more lasting. Here, "put off" means something has caused you to develop a long-term dislike or aversion to something.

Examples:

  • "I had food poisoning from that restaurant, and it completely put me off spicy food."
  • "His dishonesty put her off relationships for a long time."
  • "One bad teacher can put a child off reading for years."

The key difference from Meaning 2 is the depth and duration. In Meaning 2, you just lose interest in a moment. In Meaning 3, the dislike tends to stick around.
Meaning 4: To Distract Someone and Break Their Concentration

Here, "put off" means to break someone's focus or disrupt their performance. You are "pushing away" their ability to concentrate.

Examples:

  • "Stop humming! You're putting me off." (You are distracting me.)
  • "The loud crowd put the tennis player off, and she made several mistakes."
  • "Don't put me off while I'm counting — I'll have to start again."

This meaning is very common in British English and appears often in sports contexts. It's about something external interrupting your mental focus.
Meaning 5: To Avoid Someone or Delay Dealing With Them (Using Excuses)

In this meaning, you "put someone off" by giving them excuses, delays, or vague promises instead of dealing with them directly. You are pushing the person away rather than dealing with the matter.

Examples:

  • "I've been trying to speak to the manager for a week, but they keep putting me off."
  • "She didn't want to say no, so she put him off by saying she was busy."
  • "Every time I asked for my money back, he put me off with excuses."

Notice that in this meaning, the object is always a person, not a thing.
Meaning 6: To Drop Someone Off a Vehicle (Uncommon but Real)

This is a less frequent meaning, but you may encounter it. It means to let someone get off a bus, train, or other vehicle — sometimes even against their will.

Examples:

  • "The conductor put the passenger off at the next stop because he had no ticket."
  • "The driver put us off at the wrong terminal."

You are unlikely to use this meaning in everyday conversation, but it's good to recognize it.
The Grammar of "Put Off" — Very Important

"Put off" is what's called a separable phrasal verb. This means the object (the thing or person you're talking about) can go in two positions:

Position A — Object after "off":

  • "I put off the meeting."
  • "She put off her appointment."

Position B — Object between "put" and "off":

  • "I put the meeting off."
  • "She put her appointment off."

Both are equally correct. However, there is one strict rule you must never break:

If the object is a pronoun (it, him, her, them, me, us), it MUST go in the middle. It can NEVER go after "off."

✅ "I put it off." (correct)
❌ "I put off it." (wrong — never say this)

✅ "His behavior put me off." (correct)
❌ "His behavior put off me." (wrong)

This rule applies to all separable phrasal verbs in English, so remembering it here will help you across the board.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "put off" has multiple meanings, context is your best tool. Here are some quick clues:

  • If the object is a task, event, or plan → likely Meaning 1 (postpone).
  • If someone mentions feeling disgusted, repelled, or losing interest → Meaning 2 or 3.
  • If someone is talking about focus, concentration, or performance → Meaning 4.
  • If someone is being avoided or fobbed off with excuses → Meaning 5.
Common Collocations (Words Frequently Used Together With "Put Off")

Some things are very commonly "put off" in English. Knowing these combinations helps you sound natural:

  • Put off a meeting / appointment / trip / decision / task / payment / deadline / conversation / wedding
  • Put off doing homework / going to the doctor / making a call / starting a project
  • Be put off by someone's attitude / a smell / the price / bad reviews / a rude comment
Quick Summary of All Meanings

1. Postpone → "I put off the meeting."
2. Discourage / repel → "The price put me off buying it."
3. Cause lasting dislike → "That incident put me off flying forever."
4. Distract / break concentration → "Stop talking — you're putting me off."
5. Avoid someone with excuses → "They kept putting me off."
6. Drop off a vehicle → "The driver put them off at the station." (rare)
A Final Note on Tone

"Put off" in all its meanings carries a slightly negative or reluctant feeling. Postponing something usually implies you don't want to deal with it. Being put off means something has disappointed or repelled you. Being put off by someone means they failed to handle you properly. This underlying negativity is the emotional thread that runs through every meaning, and recognizing it will help you use "put off" with exactly the right nuance every time.
13097:
To put one's finger on something means to identify or pinpoint exactly what something is — especially when that thing is unclear, vague, or hard to define.

Think of it this way: imagine a map spread out on a table, and someone asks, "Where is the problem?" Instead of waving your hand over a wide area, you press your finger on the exact spot. That physical act of pointing to the precise location is the image behind this idiom. Mentally, it means the same thing — finding the exact thing, not just a general idea of it.
The Two Ways It Is Used

This idiom is used in two situations, and understanding both is important.

1. When you successfully identify something

Here, you managed to figure out the exact thing — a problem, a cause, a difference, or a feeling.

"After hours of thinking, she finally put her finger on what was wrong with the plan."
(= She finally identified the exact problem.)

"The doctor put his finger on the cause of the patient's illness immediately."
(= The doctor identified the exact cause.)

2. When you are struggling to identify something (the more common use)

Here, you sense that something is there — a feeling, a problem, something odd — but you cannot name or define it precisely. This form almost always uses the word "can't" or "couldn't."

"Something about his story feels wrong, but I can't put my finger on it."
(= I sense something is off, but I can't identify exactly what it is.)

"There's something different about this painting today. I just can't put my finger on it."
(= I notice a difference, but I can't pinpoint what it is.)

This second use is extremely common in everyday English, and if you only remember one form, remember: "I can't put my finger on it."
What Kind of Things Is It Used For?

This idiom is almost always used for abstract things — things you cannot physically touch. These include:

  • A problem ("I can't put my finger on the problem.")
  • A feeling ("I can't put my finger on this strange feeling.")
  • A reason ("She couldn't put her finger on why she felt so uncomfortable.")
  • A difference ("Something changed between them. I can't put my finger on what.")
  • A mistake or error ("He read the report twice but couldn't put his finger on the mistake.")

You would not normally use this idiom for something you can literally point at physically. It's for things that live in the mind — feelings, ideas, causes, reasons.

The idiom follows this pattern:

Subject + put/can't put + possessive + finger + on + it/something/what/why/the [noun]

Here are the variations:

  • I can't put my finger on it. (most common)
  • She finally put her finger on the problem.
  • They couldn't put their fingers on what was different.
  • Can you put your finger on why this doesn't feel right?
  • He put his finger on the exact moment things went wrong.

Notice how the possessive changes depending on who is doing it: my, your, his, her, their, our.

What makes this idiom so useful is that it captures a very specific human experience — that frustrating feeling when you know something is there, you can almost feel it, but you just cannot name it. Like when a word is on the tip of your tongue, or when a movie looks familiar but you can't remember where you've seen it. That experience of almost-but-not-quite knowing is exactly what "I can't put my finger on it" expresses — and no single ordinary word captures it quite as well.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The idiom comes from the literal, physical action of pressing your finger on an exact spot — like pointing to a precise location on a map, or touching a specific line in a book. When you put your finger on something physically, you are being exact and precise. Over time, this idea of physical precision was borrowed into mental and intellectual situations — "putting your finger on" an idea, a problem, or a feeling means finding the exact mental equivalent of that pinpoint.

Knowing similar expressions will help you understand this one more deeply.

  • "Figure out" — more general; means to solve or understand something. "I figured out the problem" just means you solved it. "Put my finger on the problem" specifically means you identified and named the exact issue with precision.
  • "Pin down" — very similar; means to identify or define something that keeps escaping definition. "I can't pin down what's bothering me." The difference is subtle — pin down often implies something that is moving or changing, while put your finger on implies something that is vague or elusive.
  • "Zero in on" — means to focus your attention toward something and identify it. It has more of a sense of actively searching and narrowing down. "The detective zeroed in on the suspect."
  • "Nail it down" — means to define or confirm something precisely. Slightly more forceful in tone than put your finger on.

Among all of these, "I can't put my finger on it" is the most commonly used in natural, everyday conversation.

SituationExample

At work: "There's something off about this report, but I can't put my finger on what it is."

In a relationship: "He felt something had changed between them, but he couldn't put his finger on it."

About food: "This dish tastes strange. I can't put my finger on which ingredient is wrong."

About a person: "She reminds me of someone. I just can't put my finger on who."

In medicine: "After running several tests, the doctor finally put her finger on the diagnosis."

About yourself: "I've been feeling uneasy all day, but I can't put my finger on why."

If you want to remember this idiom for life, hold onto this image:

Someone pointing with one finger at the exact spot on a map — not waving at the whole map, not pointing to a general area, but pressing one finger on the precise location.

That precision — that "exact-ness" — is the heart of this idiom. Whether you found it ("I put my finger on it") or you're still searching ("I can't put my finger on it") — the idiom is always about the quest for pinpoint identification.
13098:
Imagine a child who keeps asking their parent to stay up past bedtime. Night after night, the parent gives in. But one night, the parent says firmly: "No. Bedtime is 9 PM and that is final. I am not changing my mind." That parent has put their foot down.

"Put one's foot down" means to make a firm, final decision and refuse to change it, no matter what. It is about asserting authority or taking a strong stand on something.

This idiom has two distinct meanings. You must know both.

Meaning 1: To be firm and refuse to allow something (the main, most common meaning)

This is what most people mean when they use this idiom. When someone puts their foot down, they:

  • Take a clear, strong position on something
  • Refuse to negotiate, compromise, or back down
  • Use their authority to stop or demand something

The person is essentially saying: "This is where I draw the line. I will not tolerate or accept this any further."

Examples:

  • "My teenage son wanted to skip school every Friday, but I put my foot down and told him absolutely not."
  • "The employees kept arriving late every day, so the manager finally put her foot down and warned that it would affect their salaries."
  • "She had been letting her friend borrow money for months without getting it back. She finally put her foot down and said no more."
  • "The government put its foot down on illegal dumping and started handing out heavy fines."

Notice that in all these examples, the person using the idiom has authority over the situation — they are a parent, a manager, a friend with a boundary, or a government. Putting your foot down means you have the power to enforce what you are saying.

Meaning 2: To press the accelerator and speed up (used in British English, especially)

This is a much more literal and physical meaning. In driving, your foot presses down on the accelerator pedal to make the car go faster. So "put your foot down" simply means to accelerate or drive faster.

Examples:

  • "We're going to be late — put your foot down!"
  • "As soon as we got onto the highway, he put his foot down and the car shot forward."

This meaning is more common in British English than American English. In American English, people are more likely to say "step on it" or "floor it" for the same idea.

In everyday conversation, unless someone is clearly talking about driving, assume they are using Meaning 1.
Where Does This Idiom Come From?

The origin of Meaning 1 is rooted in body language and human behavior. When someone is angry, serious, or commanding, they often stamp or plant their foot firmly on the ground. Think of a general standing firm on a battlefield, or a person literally stomping their foot to show they will not budge. The foot is on the ground — solid, heavy, immovable. That image of firmness and refusal to move is where the idiom gets its meaning.

For Meaning 2, the origin is straightforward — it literally describes the physical act of pressing your foot onto the car's accelerator pedal.
The Feeling and Tone Behind the Idiom

When someone "puts their foot down," there is almost always a story leading up to it. This idiom implies that the person has been patient for a while, but has now reached their limit. There is a sense of:

  • Enough is enough.
  • I have been lenient, but no more.
  • My decision is made and it is non-negotiable.

This is why you'll often hear it used with words like "finally" or "eventually":

  • "She finally put her foot down."
  • "He eventually put his foot down."

These words confirm that patience ran out before the person acted firmly.

You'll hear this idiom in everyday, informal conversations — between friends, family members, and colleagues. It is not overly formal or overly casual. It sits comfortably in the middle, which means it works in most situations — at home, at work, and in general discussions.

It is used when talking about:

  • Parenting — "She put her foot down about screen time."
  • Relationships — "He put his foot down about going to the party."
  • Workplace situations — "The boss put her foot down about the dress code."
  • Personal boundaries — "I put my foot down and stopped letting people take advantage of me."
  • Politics and authority — "The prime minister put his foot down on immigration reform."

The idiom works with many subjects. Here are the patterns:

  • I / You / He / She / We / They + put(s) their foot down
  • "She put her foot down."
  • "He needs to put his foot down."
  • "I finally put my foot down."
  • "The school put its foot down on bullying."

Notice that the possessive (my, his, her, its, their) changes depending on the subject, but the idiom itself stays the same.

Because the word "foot" is in this idiom, beginners sometimes confuse it with other foot-related idioms. Here is a quick heads-up:

  • "Put your foot in your mouth" — This means to say something embarrassing or socially awkward by accident. It has nothing to do with authority or firmness. (Example: "I put my foot in my mouth when I forgot his wife's name.")
  • "Get off on the wrong foot" — This means to start a relationship or situation badly. (Example: "We got off on the wrong foot when I arrived late to our first meeting.")
  • "Have one foot in the grave" — This means to be very old or very ill, close to death.

None of these mean "put one's foot down." Keep them separate in your mind.

Main meaningTo firmly refuse something or insist that a decision is final
Second meaningTo press the accelerator and drive faster (mostly British English)
ToneFirm, authoritative, decisive
Implied backstoryThe person has tolerated something for too long and is now taking a stand
RegisterInformal to neutral — works in most everyday contexts
One Final Example to Cement It All

"For years, Marcus let his roommate leave dirty dishes in the sink without saying anything. He didn't want to cause trouble. But after months of coming home to a messy kitchen, Marcus finally put his foot down. He sat his roommate down and said clearly: 'This stops today. Either you clean up after yourself or we need to find a new living arrangement.' His roommate was surprised but agreed immediately."

In this story, Marcus was patient for a long time. He had finally had enough. He took a firm stand and made his position absolutely clear. He was not angry or aggressive — just firm and non-negotiable. That is exactly what "put one's foot down" looks like in real life.
13099: "Put out" is a phrasal verb — a combination of a verb ("put") and a small word ("out") that together create a new meaning, often very different from the individual words alone. It's one of the most versatile phrasal verbs in English, with many distinct meanings. The correct meaning always depends on context.
1. To Extinguish (a Fire, Flame, or Light)

This is the most literal and common meaning. When you "put out" a fire, you stop it from burning.

Examples:

  • "The firefighters put out the fire in an hour."
  • "Please put out your cigarette before entering."
  • "She put out the candles after dinner."

Think of it this way: a fire is "going." You push it "out of existence." You put it out.
2. To Cause Inconvenience to Someone

If you "put someone out," you cause them trouble, extra effort, or discomfort — usually by asking them to do something for you.

Examples:

  • "I don't want to put you out — I can manage on my own."
  • "He felt bad about putting his hosts out by arriving so late."
  • "Am I putting you out if I ask you to pick me up?"

This is a polite and common phrase. When someone says "please don't put yourself out," they mean: "please don't go to any extra trouble for me."
3. To Feel Annoyed or Bothered (Adjective Form)

When someone is put out, they feel irritated, offended, or upset — usually because they were inconvenienced or disrespected.

Examples:

  • "She was quite put out when no one thanked her for cooking."
  • "He seemed put out by the last-minute change of plans."
  • "I could tell she was put out, even though she didn't say anything."

Notice the structure here: "to be put out" (adjective). The person feels a mild, simmering annoyance — not explosive anger, but quiet frustration or hurt pride.
4. To Release, Publish, or Produce Something

When a company, artist, or organization "puts out" something, they release or publish it for the public.

Examples:

  • "The band put out their third album last year."
  • "The government put out an official statement this morning."
  • "The company put out a new version of their software."
  • "She has put out three novels since 2020."

This is very commonly used in journalism, music, business, and entertainment. It simply means: to send something out into the world.
5. To Place Something Outside / To Make Someone Leave

When you put something — or someone — "out," you move them to the outside, away from an interior space.

Examples:

  • "Could you put out the rubbish before you go to bed?" (take the trash outside)
  • "She put the cat out every night." (let the cat outside)
  • "He was put out of the game for fighting." (removed/ejected)

This is very common in British English for tasks like taking out the bins (garbage cans).
6. To Extend a Body Part

When you "put out" your hand, foot, or arm, you stretch or extend it outward.

Examples:

  • "He put out his hand to introduce himself."
  • "She put out her foot and tripped him accidentally."
  • "The officer put out his arm to stop the crowd."

This is a simple, physical use — you are projecting a part of your body outward.
7. To Produce or Generate (Power, Energy, or Output)

Machines, engines, or systems can "put out" a certain amount of energy, heat, or power.

Examples:

  • "This engine puts out 300 horsepower."
  • "The heater puts out enough warmth for the whole room."
  • "How much electricity does this solar panel put out?"

This is technical but very commonly used in everyday conversation when talking about machines or devices.
8. To Dislocate a Part of Your Body

If you "put out" your shoulder, your knee, or your back, you injure it by displacing it from its normal position.

Examples:

  • "He put out his back lifting those heavy boxes."
  • "She put out her shoulder during the game."
  • "Be careful — you'll put out your knee jumping like that."

This use is especially common in British and Australian English.
9. To Set Sail / Leave a Port (Nautical)

A ship or boat "puts out" when it departs from shore and heads out to sea.

Examples:

  • "The fishing boats put out at dawn."
  • "The ship put out from the harbor despite the storm warnings."

This is a traditional seafaring expression. You may encounter it in literature, news, or conversations about sailing.
10. In Baseball: To Retire a Batter or Runner

In baseball, when a fielder causes a batter or runner to be declared "out," we say the player was "put out." The noun form is a putout.

Example:

  • "The shortstop put out the runner at second base."
  • "He had three putouts in that inning."
11. The Informal/Slang Meaning (Adults)

In informal, casual American English, "put out" can refer to someone being willing to have sex. It is considered slang and is typically used in a crude or blunt way.

Example:

  • "He complained that she wouldn't put out."

You will encounter this in movies, TV shows, and casual conversation. It is not polite or formal language. Knowing it helps you understand what people mean when you hear or read it in informal contexts.
Grammar: How "Put Out" Works

Separable phrasal verb: In most of its meanings, the object (the noun) can go either between "put" and "out," or after "out."

  • "Put out the fire." ✅
  • "Put the fire out." ✅

However, when the object is a pronoun (it, him, her, them), it must go in the middle:

  • "Put it out." ✅
  • "Put out it." ❌

Intransitive use (no object): In a few meanings — especially the nautical use and the slang use — "put out" needs no object.

  • "The ship put out." ✅ (no object needed)
Quick Summary of All Meanings

• Extinguish → Put out a fire/candle/light
  • Inconvenience → I hope I'm not putting you out
  • Feel annoyed → She was put out by his behavior
  • Release/publish → The artist put out a new song
  • Place outside → Put out the trash / put the cat out
  • Extend a body part → He put out his hand
  • Generate power → The engine puts out 400 horsepower
  • Dislocate → She put out her shoulder
  • Depart by sea → The ship put out at sunrise
  • Baseball retirement → The runner was put out at third
  • Slang (adult) → Willing to have sex (crude, informal)

The key to mastering "put out" — like all phrasal verbs — is context. Once you notice whether the speaker is talking about a fire, a person's feelings, a ship, a machine, or a music album, the meaning will almost always be obvious.
